chapter: Blues, cabarets and the Golden Room
title: Who played blues before records; holes in the wall and Storyville
summary: Barnes names Bechet, Dodds, Blind Charlie and Kaiser as blues men in small bands in district cabarets, with no cutting contests, and mentions the clarinetists and trumpeters of the time.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

Well, I'm thinking, you know, on records, Bechet and Johnny Dodds played the blues good in the 20s and way back then, you know. But I wondered who was playing the blues before the records were ever made and did well on it, on the clarinet.
Really, I don't know about it because I'm trying to think now. I don't believe there must be caught in all the records. Yeah, well that's what I say.
Before they started making records, who could play good blues?

Well, as far as I can say, Bechet and myself, we was more than Tumpman. What do we call it? Tumpman. I was in a four piece band up in the hole in the walls and there, you know. Would they have any cutting contests or anything in there?

No, there wasn't any contests in there. The only trouble they had in there was old pianists, drummers, trumpets sometimes. Get up there, you had a man come in and pick a face and start playing. That's all I could say.
Would they have two clarinets at once ever?

Two clarins, two trumpets, sometimes two pianos. Not two pianos, but two mandolin pianos. All musicians, Sineviché, myself, and how they call them, Red, Red Island, Robert Taylor, all school musicians. Don Emanuel, Pickles, Teal, Rocky. Oh man, I couldn't call him anymore. I think for now, I know a lot of my twain. All them boys would be on there.
